id: A Song of a Young Lady to Her Ancient Lover

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Ancient person, for whom I All the flattering youth defy, Long be it ere thou grow old, Aching, shaking, crazy, cold; But still continue as thou art, Ancient person of my heart. On thy withered lips and dry, Which like barren furrows lie, Brooding kisses I will pour Shall thy youthful [heat] restore (Such kind showers in autumn fall, And a second spring recall); Nor from thee will ever part, Ancient person of my heart. Thy nobler part, which but to name In our sex would be counted shame, By age’s frozen grasp possessed, From [his] ice shall be released, And soothed by my reviving hand, In former warmth and vigor stand. All a lover’s wish can reach For thy joy my love shall teach, And for they pleasure shall improve All that art can add to love. Yet still I love thee without art, Ancient person of my heart.

outputs.L2:
Old beloved, I reject  
Every charming youth for you.  
May many years pass before age leaves you  
Sore, trembling, frail, and chilled;  
Remain instead the one you are,  
My cherished elder.

Upon your parched, faded mouth,  
Ridged like empty, uncultivated fields,  
I will lavish lingering kisses  
To awaken the fire of youth again—  
As gentle autumn rain  
Can summon another spring.  
I will never leave your side,  
My cherished elder.

That more intimate part of you,  
Which modest women dare not mention,  
Now held captive in age’s icy grip,  
My life-giving touch will free,  
Restoring its former heat and strength.  
My love will discover and teach  
Everything desire can offer for your delight,  
And every skill will be refined  
To deepen your pleasure.  
Yet my devotion itself needs no technique:  
You are the old beloved of my heart.
outputs.L3: The speaker rejects the flattering attention of younger admirers, declaring her preference for an elderly beloved. She wishes that he might remain as he is, untouched by the increasing weakness, pain, and indignities of old age. Her affection, she suggests, possesses a rejuvenating power: her kisses will restore warmth and vitality to him, just as autumn rain can awaken the earth into a second spring. She promises to revive the sexual vigor that age has diminished and to devote herself fully to his pleasure. Yet although she is willing to employ all the arts and techniques of love, she emphasizes that her devotion is neither calculated nor artificial. It arises from genuine desire and sincere affection.
outputs.L4:
The speaker turns away from the flattering attention of younger admirers and directs his devotion instead toward an elderly beloved. He does not deny the signs of age or the decline of physical strength; rather, he addresses them with tenderness, confidence, and openly erotic affection. Through intimate imagery, he promises that his touch, experience, and loving care can rekindle the beloved’s fading warmth, awaken desire, and restore something of his former vitality.

At the poem’s heart is a celebration of constancy. Genuine love, the speaker suggests, is not dependent on youth, beauty, or bodily vigor. It remains faithful even when time has altered the beloved’s appearance and diminished his powers. Although the fantasy of erotic renewal imagines affection as capable of reversing age’s effects, the deeper claim is that sincere devotion already transcends physical decline. Love does not merely seek a youthful body; it cherishes the whole person and finds dignity, pleasure, and beauty in enduring attachment.
outputs.L5: Long ago, when all the world seemed young, an ancient tree stood alone upon a hill. Its roots held forgotten stories, and its branches reached toward the stars. Travelers often rested beneath it, believing that anyone who listened closely could hear the wisdom of ages carried through its leaves.

Ancient person, for whom I  
All the flattering youth defy,  
Long be it ere thou grow old,  
Aching, shaking, crazy cold;  
But still continue as thou art,  
Ancient person of my heart.

On thy withered lips and dry,  
Which like barren furrows lie,  
Brooding kisses I will pour,  
Shall thy youthful heat restore:  
Such kind showers in autumn fall,  
And a second spring recall;  
Nor from thee will ever part,  
Ancient person of my heart.

Thy nobler part, which but to name  
In our sex would be counted shame,  
By age’s frozen grasp possessed,  
From its ice shall be released,  
And, soothed by my reviving hand,  
In former warmth and vigor stand:  
All a lover’s wish can reach,  
For thy joy my love shall teach;  
And for thy pleasure shall improve  
All that art can add to love:  
Yet still I love thee without art,  
Ancient person of my heart.
